One pass may now correct at most `min(10, ceil(25% of active rows))` rows, oldest first, with everything over the cap keeping its confirmed two-pass standing for a later pass instead of restarting its clock; and "an empty listing is never evidence" is now asserted of BOTH observations rather than only the current one, by threading the previous pass's listed/not-listed fact in explicitly instead of leaving it to fall out of the caller clearing its set. `(CURATION-PROVENANCE)` makes the filter itself legible from the wire: every `/v1/tree` now carries an OPTIONAL `curation` object (enabled, mirror age, how many workspaces it removed), because an empty or short tree had two indistinguishable causes — nothing is running, or the mirror filtered it away — and only the second is a bug shape. Optional by contract, since both shipped clients must keep parsing a newer bridge. `(EMIT-OPTIONAL-FIELDS)` closes the same gap for three facts the bridge already held and never sent: a project/workspace `pinned` flag (pinning is the one act of curation that changes ORDER rather than membership, so a filter that only decides what to hide could not carry it, and `pinned_at`/`is_pinned` had been SELECTed and read by nothing; it is OMITTED rather than sent as `false` when curation is disabled, because §7.2 distinguishes a field the bridge does not report from one it reports as not-pinned, and a renderer that has never synced is not evidence that nothing is pinned), and `questionCount` + `multiSelect` on a pending-question ref — the headline is only the FIRST question's header, so a 3-question capture rendered exactly like a 1-question one, and a multi-select item has its own byte contract that single-select affordances would offer and the bridge would then refuse. The two filters have OPPOSITE failure directions from the guards they sit beside and that is deliberate: an unfilled mirror, an unmirrored workspace, an unreachable daemon or a stale snapshot all resolve to SHOWING the row, because hiding a real blocked agent is the one failure the feature cannot absorb — while the answer path consults neither liveness nor curation after resolving the captured terminal target, so a question captured before its thread was snoozed stays answerable. `(QUESTION-EXPIRY)` closes the same hole for questions: a pending question on a terminal that no longer exists is settled `stale` and its push retracted through the existing settled-ids wiring, instead of buzzing, counting toward `oldestUnansweredMs` and holding a slot forever. It is held to a HIGHER bar than the tree filter beside it, because `settle(stale)` is terminal and the retraction pulls a notification off the phone: it reads a strict `isProvablyGone` (never `!isLive`) that refuses to read anything into an empty daemon listing at any age — the reaper's rule, not the tree's — passes the row's own `last_attached_at ?? created_at` so a terminal born after the snapshot cannot lose that race, and requires the same verdict on two separate reconcile passes five minutes apart. A flap, an unreachable daemon or a stale snapshot resets the clock rather than condemning anything. The same strict predicate gates the push sender's fire-time re-check, whose `forget()` is equally one-shot: an uncertain verdict there keeps the buzz. `(BRIDGE-AGENT-KIND)` keeps read-side classification consistent: the kind falls back from nullable `definition_id` to the hook's exact `agent_id`. It is not an answer preflight — `(ANSWER-GUARDLESS)` deliberately writes to the captured Claude question's terminal without re-reading mutable binding evidence. Two whole-mirror gates sit in front of every per-row rule, both returning the SAME pass-through curation the bootstrap case does, because a mirror that is not evidence about this machine's sidebar right now must not be filtered with. `(MIRROR-AGE-OUT)` refuses a mirror whose last sync is over 20 minutes old — four of the writer's five-minute heartbeats, so only a genuinely absent renderer reaches it — because every hiding field in those tables is then an opinion from a session that has ended, and `snooze_launch_id` in particular keeps hiding threads the very next launch would have released, with nothing left to release them. `(MIRROR-ORG-GATE)` refuses a mirror written for a different organization: `host.db` is per machine and the mirror inside it is per org, the column had been written and read since the mirror shipped without ever being compared, and since ids do not collide across orgs the practical effect was the project gate hiding the ENTIRE tree. `(PUSH-CURATION-GATE)` extends the same curation to the one companion side effect that never passed through the read API: arming hangs off the capture sink, so a binned, archived, completed or snoozed thread still buzzed the WATCH and the notification then opened a tree that did not contain it — snooze worst of all, since "not now" is exactly a statement about being interrupted. It is asked at FIRE time, on every sweep, rather than once before `schedule` — and that is the correctness of the gate, not a detail of where it sits. Curation is REVOCABLE (a snooze expires by itself; an archive or a bin is undone by hand) while `armPush` runs exactly once, at capture, so declining to arm turned a twenty-minute snooze into six hours of silence for a question the sidebar had long since put back, with no fence row left for anything to reconsider and the tree still showing the question the whole time. Every capture is armed now, restart reconstruction covers all of them unchanged, and the sweep decides only whether THIS sweep may fire, so the buzz lands on the first sweep after the curation lapses. The curation hold and the presence hold are independent `continue`s over the same armed entry — whichever holds, holds, and neither can release what the other is still holding — and both sit ABOVE the one-shot `isStillUnanswered` branch, so the one input that is EXPECTED to change its mind is never answered at the point where the only outcomes are fire-now or forget-forever. Answering is still the only permanent disarm. Every uncertain answer BUZZES: curation disabled, no `workspaces` row, a question the memory-only store has never seen (the restart case, which `isStillUnanswered` owns and logs), or anything thrown while asking, and only a positive non-`show` verdict from an enabled curation holds — cached for `CURATION_RECHECK_MS` and logged once per HOLD EPISODE rather than 1,800 times an hour, because a 2 s sweep over a 6 h hold would otherwise mean ~10,800 synchronous reads of the whole mirror per question and as many identical log lines | `(BRIDGE-SIDEBAR-FILTER)`, `(BRIDGE-LIVENESS)`, `(QUESTION-EXPIRY)`, `(BRIDGE-AGENT-KIND)`, `(MIRROR-AGE-OUT)`, `(MIRROR-ORG-GATE)`, `(PUSH-CURATION-GATE)`, `(REAPER-CORRECTION-CAP)`, `(CURATION-PROVENANCE)`, `(EMIT-OPTIONAL-FIELDS)` |
85	| Tree freshness the phone can trust | the phone stamps its list 'updated just now' when a heartbeat comes back with `treeStale == false` and counts matching the tree it holds — the desktop asserting, live, that a refetch would return what is already on screen. `treeStale` is derived from `gseq`, and `gseq` moved for exactly ONE reason: a question RESOLVING. So a NEW question was invisible to it, and the counts beside it do not always move either, because `deriveSessionStatus` already reports `needs_input` for a terminal whose binding is latched on `PermissionRequest` — the state left behind by `(QUESTION-EXPIRY)` settling a question stale, or by the window after a desk answer before the next hook event lands. A capture on such a terminal changed nothing either signal could see, so the phone confidently asserted freshness over a list with no tappable card for a live blocked agent, indefinitely. Every transition of the pending set now mints the protocol frame that describes it — `question.pending` on capture, `question.resolved` or `question.stale` on a reconcile settle — so `gseq` moves whenever the tree's most important content does. The frames invent nothing: the resolved branch reads back the provenance the store already stamped and reports `outcome: unknown`, which is the honest member (a `tool_result` proves the tool call ended, not that a human chose an option), the stale branch names the one reason `(QUESTION-EXPIRY)` settles on, and a summary whose terminal no longer resolves in host.db is dropped rather than published with a guessed handle. `answerable` on a broadcast frame is evaluated against `BRIDGE_CAPABILITIES`, because a frame has no device — the per-device narrowing is §9.2's snapshot. A capture is published even when `(PUSH-CURATION-GATE)` will hold the push for it: the two gates answer different questions, and both fail toward telling the user more rather than less. Neither publish can throw into its caller: a capture that succeeded must not become a 500, and a retraction must not be lost, over a freshness signal | `(TREE-FRESHNESS-GSEQ)` |
86	| A retraction that survives the trip | §13's `x` is one field with one meaning and the client applies it BEFORE it reads `k`: `isExpired(now)` discards the frame, so a retraction stamped with `now` was expired on arrival by construction and every notification it was sent to clear survived on the handset. The retract frame now carries its own TTL measured from creation — a day, sized to outlive a phone that was off the network, in Doze or powered down when the answer landed, and safe to over-size because the client independently drops a retraction naming a notification it no longer shows | `(RETRACT-TTL)` |
87	| One choke point for a settled question | a settled question is exactly the moment any notification about it must be pulled off the phone (§13.3), and that wiring hung off individual call sites: the desk-answer sink retracted and the reconcile path retracted, while the two remaining routes out of `pending` did not. A REMOTE answer — the whole point of the feature — resolved the record and returned, so the watch kept buzzing about the question the user had just answered ON it; and a SUPERSEDE marked the prior record stale by writing the field directly, leaving a notification pointing at a question the tree had already dropped. `retract()` had zero production callers. Every ending now passes through `settle()`, the only writer of a terminal state, which calls one sink the composition root wires to `push.cancelPending` — so a settle route added later cannot forget, because there is nowhere else to write `resolved`/`stale`. The sink is required, not optional, so a composition root that omits it fails to compile rather than running silent; and a sink that throws is caught and logged rather than propagated, because settling has already happened by then and on the answer path the caller has already typed into a terminal | `(SETTLE-CHOKE-POINT)` |
88	| A backwards clock cannot latch a hold | two caches in the push path bounded their freshness from ABOVE only, so a wall-clock step backwards (NTP correction, resume) made a stamp the clock has not reached yet read as maximally fresh — and both caches only ever hold things that SUPPRESS. The curation probe's per-question row latched a HOLD, silencing a question whose snooze had already lapsed for as long as the step lasted; and `(MIRROR-AGE-OUT)`'s window — the only thing standing between the phone and a mirror left behind by a renderer that has since quit — passed a future stamp forever, so a quit desktop went on hiding threads from the phone. Negative age is now a cache MISS and an AGE-OUT respectively: each fails in the direction its own contract already names, which is toward buzzing and toward showing | `(CLOCK-STEP-FAILS-OPEN)` |
89	| The hook does not choose a question's workspace | capture stored `input.workspaceId` — a field of an unauthenticated localhost POST — even though `resolveActiveTerminal` had just returned that terminal's `host_workspace_id` from host.db two statements earlier. That id decides which thread the phone opens and is the one `(PUSH-CURATION-GATE)` asks curation about, so a wrong claim buzzes about, and opens, another thread. The derived value is stored and a mismatch is logged with the claim beside it — the same rule `(TRANSCRIPT-PATH-DERIVED)` already applies to the other field the hook also claims | `(HOOK-CLAIM-NOT-TRUSTED)` |
90	| A gone terminal must be seen twice | the push sender's fire-time re-check answered one boolean for two different facts, and acted on both the same way: `forget()` dropped the fence row, so a question dropped on ONE daemon observation could never buzz again, at any later moment, for any reason — and it happened silently. Everything else in this feature holds an irreversible verdict to two observations (`reconcile` before `settle(stale)`, the reaper before correcting a row); this path did not. The check now answers a VERDICT: `settled` is a fact about the record and is acted on at once, while `gone` is one fallible listing and becomes a HOLD — like presence and curation, and asked while the entry is still armed — until the same verdict comes back `PUSH_GONE_CORROBORATION_MS` later, at which point the drop is LOGGED. A terminal that reads live again resets the clock to zero, so a flapping or mid-restart daemon can never accumulate its way to a drop | `(PUSH-GONE-CORROBORATION)` |

# Fork feature manifest

This file is the source of truth for **what our fork adds on top of upstream
superset**. The nightly upstream-merge workflow greps every marker below against
the merged tree; **if any marker is missing the merge is rejected** (a feature
was dropped or an upstream change clobbered it) and the build hard-aborts into
the recovery loop. Markers are deliberately distinctive identifiers that only
exist because of our feature code.

When you add a new custom feature, add a marker row here in the same commit.
When upstream **deprecates/removes** a feature we mirrored, remove its marker row
in the merge that drops it (the only legitimate way a marker leaves this list).

## Features

| Feature | What it is | Marker |
|---|---|---|
| Native Windows ARM64 packaging | one-click NSIS installer; ARM64 node-pty/libsql/tokenizers | `npm:@lydell/node-pty`, `bun-windows-arm64` |
| Window controls | native `titleBarOverlay` is the sole min/max/close set on Windows | `titleBarOverlay` |
| Windows behaviour fixes | child-process patch, cmd.exe fallback, force-foreground, watchdog, WebGL recovery, fast startup | `windows-child-process` |
| Agent status dots (Claude + Codex) | per-terminal dot + workspace rollup; host-service POST + JSONL watcher | `pane-map-hook`, `StatusIndicator` |
| Companion lifecycle alerts | phone + custom watch receive distinct ready-for-review and terminal-agent-failure notifications; ready fires once per real work cycle, tool/subagent/admin failures are excluded, and presence/sidebar curation match blocked-agent push behavior | `(COMPANION-LIFECYCLE-ALERTS)` |
| Claude Stop unhooked from notify.sh | upstream's raw Stop passthrough must never race superset-notify.py (it wiped the blue dot + yellow-hold) | `CLAUDE-STOP-UNHOOKED` |
| Compaction shows working | Claude context compaction (manual /compact + auto) drives the yellow dot via PreCompact / SessionStart(source=compact) | `(COMPACT-YELLOW)` |
| Team/workflow work shows working | background_tasks[] entry types split the post-turn dot: agent-type work (teammate/subagent/workflow) holds yellow; shell-only goes blue | `(TEAM-YELLOW)` |
| Codex-companion job holds the dot | detached codex worker is invisible to background_tasks[]; an active (pid-alive) codex job for the session holds yellow incl. through StopFailure AND the JSONL watcher's user-interrupt turn-end (System 1 mirrors the same check via `codexJobActive` in agent-jsonl-watcher.ts, so a codex-only session can't false-green when the user interrupts the Claude turn — the codex worker is a separate process on its own API and keeps running) | `_codex_job_active` |
| Manual compact restores shell-blue | a manual /compact ending while only a background shell runs restores the BackgroundRunning blue (turn-end snapshot marker) instead of false-greening; the JSONL-watcher re-attach after compaction must not wipe that blue | `_shellbg_marker_path`, `(BLUE-SPECTATOR)` |
| Watcher ignores replayed and counterfeit turn-ends | the JSONL watcher emits ONE turn-end of its own — a user interrupt — because Claude Code fires no hook for it; every other turn-end, including a terminal API error, is the hook's (Claude Code runs its StopFailure hooks whenever the turn's last record is an api-error and superset-notify.py's StopFailure branch answers `Stop`), so hook-is-truth holds and the watcher's api-error contribution is auto-resume signalling only, which asserts no dot state. The watcher's own emit still bypasses superset-notify.py, and the renderer clears the background-running axis on every non-`BackgroundRunning` agent event, so a `Stop` fired off the wrong line wipes the blue the hook just restored (live: compact-end `BackgroundRunning`, then 763ms later the watcher re-parsed the compaction-rewritten transcript, matched a HISTORICAL "Request interrupted by user" and greened the dot under a still-running background shell). Two gates now stand between a matched line and an emit. FIRST, the line must BE an interrupt: the marker was a raw PHRASE match, and this repo's own agent traffic quotes it constantly — measured over 10,695 local transcripts the phrase predicate matched 1217 lines of which 70 were quotes (tool_results and long teammate messages), and 9 of the 10 interrupt-releases in a live log window were false `Stop`s fired MID-TURN. So it is parsed to Claude Code's EXACT synthetic record — a user entry whose message content is a single `text` block equal to `[Request interrupted by user]` — which drops every quote and keeps all 1147 genuine records. SECOND, the turn must have ended JUST NOW: Claude Code re-presents already-written entries (compaction rewrite, post-truncation re-read from offset 0, discover-poll whole-file read), so each entry is replay-gated on its own `uuid` (already judged → never counts again, at any age) and `timestamp` age, which must be no older than 120s and no further in the future than a 5s clock-skew tolerance (a backward NTP step would otherwise make ALL history read as fresh). A file that already existed when the watcher started is never replayed whole through a cold gate, but it is no longer tailed blind either: Codex seeds it to EOF, and Claude re-reads a bounded 256KB tail under a third gate layer — a pre-start fence suppressing every entry stamped strictly before the watcher started (no skew slack: both stamps come from the same machine's clock). The fence is held on the file's own state, not a per-pass local, so a read that throws after the offset was rewound cannot make the retry re-read that history UNFENCED. Seeding blind would SWALLOW an append that landed between `fs.watch` going live and the deferred seed reaching that file, and an interrupt has no hook fallback at all, so that dot would stay stuck; the tail is bounded because reading a multi-megabyte transcript synchronously at startup is what starves the renderer. A blocked match emits NOTHING, so the hook's blue stands and an AUTO compact no longer gets a false turn-end. A genuine interrupt still emits a bare `Stop` (the (BA) blue latch has no self-clear, and the Agent-Complete chime is Stop-only), and that verdict is explicit — never derived from best-effort marker cleanup | `(WATCHER-BLUE-STOMP)` |
| ws native modules off | host-service `ws` must use pure-JS mask/unmask — a broken packaged bufferutil wedges WS receivers and kills ALL terminal keyboard input | `WS_NO_BUFFER_UTIL` |
| Shell-running blue dot | OSC 133 C/D command-running detection | `scanForOsc133Cd` |
| Non-git / multi-repo workspaces | open a non-git folder as a plain workspace | `resolveNonGitFolder` |
| Multi-repo branch workspaces | "Open from multi-folder" groups N git repos; "+" fans the same branch out as a worktree per repo under one container workspace | `readMultiRepoConfig`, `createMultiRepoWorkspaceFlow` |
| Multi-repo member management | Project Settings "Repositories" section adds/removes member repos of a multi-repo project. Add is lazy (included in NEW branch workspaces only — cleanup already tolerates a missing member worktree); remove force-removes that repo's worktrees from every existing branch container (confirm dialog; repo + branches kept) BEFORE the config rewrite so no orphan worktrees/registrations strand. Min 2 members enforced | `addMultiRepoMember`, `MultiRepoMembersSection` |
| Workspace branch label | the open workspace page names its branch top-right in the tab bar (click copies) — the only branch surface a non-git multi-repo container has | `WorkspaceBranchLabel` |
| Workspace-create failure toast | every workspace/worktree create failure raises a toast with the actual reason (e.g. a GitHub/network timeout) from the one `recordFailure` chokepoint — so a transient failure no longer reads as a silent "stuck creating → reload" | `(CREATE-FAIL-TOAST)` |
| Thread snooze / archive | per-thread timed Snooze + sticky Archive in the sidebar | `getWorkspaceSidebarBucket`, `APP_LAUNCH_ID`, `DashboardSidebarStateSection` |
| Sidebar row projection carries the fork state fields | the host-owned sidebar row projection (`rawSidebarWorkspaces` in `useDashboardSidebarData`) must carry `snoozeUntil`/`snoozeLaunchId`/`archivedAt`/`completedAt`/`deletedAt` from `v2WorkspaceLocalState` — the v1.14.2 upstream merge rebuilt that mapping and silently dropped them, which broke snooze (rows never left the active lane), emptied the Recycle Bin, vanished archived masters, and resurfaced completed threads under Archived | `(SIDEBAR-STATE-PROJECTION)` |
| Master rows snoozeable | `snoozeWorkspace` inserts a pre-snoozed local-state row for an auto-included main that has none yet (mirrors `archiveWorkspace`) — Snooze on a master row used to silently no-op | `(SNOOZE-MAIN)` |
| Sessions snooze / archive too | project-less "session" rows get the same Snooze and Archive semantics as project threads, surfaced in two top-level `Snoozed Sessions` / `Archived Sessions` subsections under the Sessions header (revealed from its right-click menu). The bucket classifier was already project-agnostic, so a snoozed or archived session simply LEFT the active lane and could never be recovered — the only surfaces that rendered an inactive row were the per-project ones, and a session has no project row to hang either the rows or the reveal/collapse flags off. The flags therefore live on the fixed-size `v2UserPreferences` singleton rather than a per-entity key, and hiding a session never navigates away from it: an open session stays open in the pane it is already in. Sessions still never reach the Kanban board — every card is bound to a sidebar project id and a session's is null | `(SESSION-LIFECYCLE)` |
| Sticky project removal | "Remove project from sidebar" tombstones EVERY workspace of the project incl. mains, and passive workspace route mounts (session restore, kanban split) use `placeWorkspaceFromPassiveMount`, which never re-inserts the project's sidebar row and never resurrects an existing hidden row — a removed project can only come back via an EXPLICIT open (Workspaces page, project setup/import) | `(REMOVE-STICKY)` |
| Case-insensitive repo-path dedupe | host-service `project.findByPath` / import-collision checks compare `projects.repoPath` case-insensitively on win32/darwin (case-insensitive filesystems) — a case-only folder rename used to miss the existing row and mint a duplicate project (cloud slug conflict suffixed `-2` instead of reusing) | `(PATH-CI-DEDUPE)` |
| Merge semantic review gate | every nightly upstream merge — clean or conflicted — is reviewed by Opus against this manifest BEFORE it may commit/build/publish: a cleanly-merging upstream hunk that semantically breaks a fork feature (the v1.14.2 sidebar-projection incident) is caught here, not in production. Review is fresh after every adaptation and fails closed: no parsable verdict, a final BREAKAGE verdict, or a review run that modified the tree all hard-abort with the baseline untouched | `(MERGE-SEMANTIC-GATE)` |
| Nightly proactive port + bounded adaptation | after conflict resolution, Opus compares the old/new upstream tag trees against fork-owned files and surgically ports cleanly-merging API refactors before the gates; semantic BREAKAGE findings then drive at most two repair rounds, each followed by ReferenceError + marker gates and a fresh review. This closes the desktop-v1.16.0 class where upstream removed collections/exports used only by fork files, so git produced no conflict for the resolver to see | `(MERGE-ADAPT)` |
| Self-repairing build | a failed ARM64 build attempt triggers a bounded Opus 5 repair loop (max 3 attempts / 2 repairs): the repair agent reads the failed job's log, fixes the checked-out tree (scripts/, .github/actions/, source — all take effect the NEXT attempt of the SAME run), and pushes to the repair branch; every deterministic gate re-runs on the repaired sha. Repairs can never change the app version or touch FEATURES.md; workflow-YAML fixes need `WORKFLOW_PUSH_TOKEN` and land next run | `(BUILD-REPAIR)` |
| Sidebar hover-freeze | rows never re-sort while the pointer is over the project list (order applies on leave) | `(HOVER-FREEZE)` |
| Terminal links | plain click copies a URL/path, Ctrl/Cmd+click opens; `.html` paths open in Chrome (OS default fallback) | `useLinkClickHint`, `openHtmlInBrowser` |
| Agent-hook bash-wrap | Gemini/Cursor `.sh` hooks run via Git-for-Windows bash | `agent-wrappers` |
| Kanban board | device-local board mirroring branches + Queued column | `v2KanbanCards`, `KANBAN_QUEUE_COLUMN_ID` |
| Kanban host-served workspace source | every fork surface that needs the workspace universe (kanban seed/prune/render, bound-card actions, collapse-split, recycle-bin destroy URL, sidebar snooze/archive fallbacks, is-local gate) reads the host-served lists (`useHostWorkspaces`), NEVER the Electric `v2Workspaces` mirror — upstream's offline-first migration stopped writing new rows to the cloud table, so Electric reads silently miss every post-migration branch | `(KANBAN-HOST-SOURCE)` |
| Kanban Completed column | fixed FINAL column: dropping a card or choosing Mark completed on an active non-main worktree stamps an editable completed date and hides the thread from the sidebar ENTIRELY (drag out un-completes/restores); per-column date filter (all / last calendar month / custom range) for work-done reports; completed cards survive branch deletion as frozen records; main cards can't complete | `KANBAN_COMPLETED_COLUMN_ID`, `(KANBAN-MARK-COMPLETED)` |
| Kanban append-only backup | daily write-once JSON snapshot of the board; code can never delete/overwrite one | `writeKanbanBackup` |
| Kanban sidebar button toggles | sidebar Kanban press: anywhere → full-screen board; part-screen split → full-screen (closing then reopens that workspace full size); full-screen → close back to the remembered previous page (fallback Workspaces list) | `(KANBAN-TOGGLE)` |
| Subagent tool events never stomp the red | a PostToolUse whose payload carries `agent_id` (ran inside a subagent) maps to the red-respecting SubagentActive — background agents' tool completions must not clear a pending AskUserQuestion/permission red; only a main-loop completion does. SubagentStart likewise | `(SUBTOOL-RED)` |
| Async background-tool completions never stomp the red | the Workflow / Agent / Task tools spawn background agents and complete on the MAIN loop (no agent_id) WHILE the main loop is blocked on an AskUserQuestion/permission red — so their PostToolUse maps to SubagentActive, not Start, instead of wrongly clearing the pending red (the SUBTOOL-RED sequential-main-loop assumption breaks for async-spawning tools) | `(ASYNC-TOOL-RED)` |
| Untagged background-agent tool completions never stomp the red | teammate/fork tool completions (ordinary Read/Bash/Edit/…) stream in attributed to the PARENT session WITHOUT an agent_id, so the SUBTOOL-RED/ASYNC-TOOL-RED checks miss them and they would Start-clear a pending AskUserQuestion red. A `<terminalId>.askq/` DIR holds one marker PER OWNER (the raising agent_id, or `_main`), set synchronously at PreToolUse:AskUserQuestion; while ANY marker exists an untagged ordinary PostToolUse maps to the red-respecting SubagentActive (and refreshes `.bgactive`, since the blocked main loop means that tool is genuine teammate activity). Per-owner so concurrent questions (main + a subagent) are independent. The renderer has ONE permission axis per terminal, so a single CENTRAL GUARD wraps the whole decision and enforces "rendered red ⇔ `.askq` dir non-empty" in one place: it counts owners before and after the inner decision, then (DOWNGRADE) turns any red-CLEARING result (Start, or a green/blue turn-end) into the red-respecting SubagentActive while any owner remains (stamping `.mainstopped` on a held turn-end so the last SubagentStop still finalizes green), and (UPGRADE) turns a NON-clearing result (SubagentActive yellow/agent/codex hold, or a None no-op) into Start when this event removed the LAST owner — so a just-answered/cancelled/reaped question's red can't latch behind a yellow hold. One choke point, so NO branch — answer, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop (incl. its cancelled-with-question and still-other-work paths), the compact paths — can drop a co-pending red OR strand a resolved one. (The native-notification manager likewise only chimes "complete" on Stop and "awaiting" on permission, never on SubagentActive.) Durability is asserted (`PRAGMA synchronous = FULL`) rather than inferred from NTFS rename ordering, and rows validate individually, so a corrupt row costs one requestId its status instead of quarantining every other record’s 24 hours. `(FREETEXT-N2-PROVEN)` widens WHERE a typed answer is accepted: free text now works on a multi-question prompt — 59% of real traffic — because the per-question sequence was driven in a pty and the agent's own `tool_result` confirmed it (the editor-closing `\r` ADVANCES to the next question rather than submitting, so a free-text question and a digit question compose and the prompt is submitted by the same review-screen return that already ends an all-digit N>1 answer). `(MSEL-N2-PROVEN)` closes the last prompt shape: a multi-select question inside an N>1 prompt is a per-question group of toggle digits terminated by the SAME right-arrow that submits a lone multi-select — there it ADVANCES (next question mid-prompt, review screen on the last) — driven first, middle and last, twice each, mixed with free-text siblings and with the zero-toggle empty group (which the CLI accepts and then OMITS from the `tool_result`, exactly as a desk submit past the review warning does). What the earlier refutation actually refuted was the N=1 submit PAIR reused verbatim: its trailing `\r` landed on the next question. The one shape still refused is refused on EVIDENCE rather than on caution: on a multi-select question the free-text row's digit toggles a checkbox, the body text is swallowed with no echo and the terminating `\r` toggles whatever row the caret was on — a run that asked for free text came back answered with the first option instead. A `\r` into a multi-select question is the single most dangerous byte this contract knows, so `assertNoReturnIntoMultiSelect` re-checks every emitted sequence against the prompt itself. The picker contract is per build AND per shape, and one build's proof can never backfill another's | `(COMPANION-BRIDGE)`, `(ANSWER-GUARDLESS)`, `(ANSWER-LEDGER)`, `(PUSH-PRESENCE)`, `(FREETEXT-N2-PROVEN)`, `(MSEL-N2-PROVEN)` |
| Sidebar-state mirror | the desktop sidebar's CURATION — which projects and threads are in it, where they sit, and whether each is hidden, archived, snoozed, completed, soft-deleted, pinned or manually reordered — lives entirely in renderer `localStorage` collections (`v2WorkspaceLocalState`, `v2SidebarProjects`) that no other process can read, while `host.db` is a lifecycle-free append store of everything the machine has ever created. Anything outside the renderer that tries to show "the user's sidebar" therefore reads a structurally different, strictly larger set in which a thread binned last month is indistinguishable from one blocked on the user right now. This projects that curation into three `host.db` tables (`sidebar_workspace_state`, `sidebar_project_state`, `sidebar_mirror_meta`) via a fork-only `sidebarMirror.sync` tRPC mutation the renderer pushes on every curation change, debounced. It is a WHOLE-SNAPSHOT replace, not a delta: curation has no single choke point (context menus, bulk actions, kanban drags, the snooze submenu, drag-reorder, the CLI worktree placer), so the only correctness condition that survives new entry points is "something changed" — which also makes a failed sync, a host-service restart and a renderer reload all self-repair on the next push. The renderer stays the source of truth and the host-service never writes these tables; the mirror is a projection with ONE permitted failure direction — an ABSENT row means "no opinion recorded" and consumers must SHOW the row (`LEFT JOIN`, never `INNER`), because hiding on absence turns a transient miss into a blocked agent nobody sees. Staleness is deliberately NOT folded into that rule: a stale row still carrying `deleted_at`/`archived_at`/`is_hidden`/`snooze_until` hides a thread the user has since restored, which is the forbidden direction, so the writer bounds it instead — exactly one push in flight (two on separate loopback connections have no ordering guarantee, and an older one served last would leave host.db behind a signature already recorded as synced, freezing the mirror until the next curation change) and a retry that never gives up while the app runs (the bounded version had a terminal state that a host-service restart on the same port could never re-arm). Identity fields are normalized rather than trusted for the same reason a localStorage row cannot be: the collections validate on WRITE only, so a legacy row hands back `undefined` behind a `string` type, and the first `.length` on one would have thrown inside the render of a hook mounted with no error boundary nearer than the root route. With the renderer gone the mirror holds the user's last recorded curation; it never invents one. `(MIRROR-HEARTBEAT)` is what makes that statement CHECKABLE from outside: the signature gate that stops identical snapshots from being re-sent also made `last_full_sync_at_ms` measure the last curation CHANGE rather than renderer liveness, so an untouched sidebar was indistinguishable from a quit app and no consumer could age the mirror out toward showing. The same unchanged snapshot is therefore re-pushed every five minutes, and a push is additionally forced whenever the last PUSHED `app_launch_id` differs from the current one — the launch id travels in the meta row, not the snapshot, so a launch whose curation serialized identically to the previous one's would otherwise leave the mirror claiming the old launch and keep every thread snoozed-until-next-launch hidden downstream. `sidebar_mirror_meta` carries the two things an outside reader cannot otherwise derive: its presence distinguishes "no renderer has ever synced" (pass everything through) from a genuinely empty curated sidebar, and its `app_launch_id` is what makes an "until next launch" snooze evaluable at all | `(SIDEBAR-MIRROR)`, `(MIRROR-HEARTBEAT)` |
| Companion tree mirrors the sidebar, not `host.db` | the bridge's three read statements were unqualified `SELECT`s, so the phone received a structurally different, strictly LARGER set than the desktop sidebar: 22/22 projects, 183/183 workspaces and 310 terminal rows, with binned, archived and snoozed threads rendering as ordinary live rows and 63 workspaces contributing an inert header with nothing under it. Two independent filters now stand between `host.db` and the wire. `(BRIDGE-SIDEBAR-FILTER)` consumes `(SIDEBAR-MIRROR)` and reproduces the renderer's own bucket classifier — deleted, completed, archived, snoozed and hidden are off the default sidebar and are therefore off the phone UNLESS they carry a pending captured question (a question pierces curation so it cannot disappear from every discovery surface), threads group under the project the user PLACED them in rather than `workspaces.project_id`, and a repo removed from the sidebar takes its threads with it. `(BRIDGE-LIVENESS)` answers the separate question of whether a `status='active'` row still names a pty that exists: it never did — a row leaves `active` only via an explicit dispose or a live in-process `onExit`, so a crash, a force-quit or a host-service restart strands it forever, and 403 such rows spanning 77 days were reaching the phone, 8 of them frozen on `PermissionRequest` and badging permanently-blocked agents that had not existed for weeks. Liveness is the same pair the host-service's own session listing joins (an in-process session, or an id the pty-daemon reports alive), snapshotted for read-side liveness filtering without daemon round trips, and the reap pass now walks row -> daemon as well as daemon -> row so `host.db` stops accumulating corpses (five independent conditions before a row is corrected, because being wrong costs a LIVE terminal its place in the desktop's own session list). `(REAPER-CORRECTION-CAP)` bounds that walk, because its two passes are not two independent observations: a degraded daemon — mid-restart, partially adopted, answering from a half-built registry — stays degraded for longer than the five minutes between them, so both listings can be the same wrong listing, and the corrective write has no undo. One pass may now correct at most `min(10, ceil(25% of active rows))` rows, oldest first, with everything over the cap keeping its confirmed two-pass standing for a later pass instead of restarting its clock; and "an empty listing is never evidence" is now asserted of BOTH observations rather than only the current one, by threading the previous pass's listed/not-listed fact in explicitly instead of leaving it to fall out of the caller clearing its set. `(CURATION-PROVENANCE)` makes the filter itself legible from the wire: every `/v1/tree` now carries an OPTIONAL `curation` object (enabled, mirror age, how many workspaces it removed), because an empty or short tree had two indistinguishable causes — nothing is running, or the mirror filtered it away — and only the second is a bug shape. Optional by contract, since both shipped clients must keep parsing a newer bridge. `(EMIT-OPTIONAL-FIELDS)` closes the same gap for three facts the bridge already held and never sent: a project/workspace `pinned` flag (pinning is the one act of curation that changes ORDER rather than membership, so a filter that only decides what to hide could not carry it, and `pinned_at`/`is_pinned` had been SELECTed and read by nothing; it is OMITTED rather than sent as `false` when curation is disabled, because §7.2 distinguishes a field the bridge does not report from one it reports as not-pinned, and a renderer that has never synced is not evidence that nothing is pinned), and `questionCount` + `multiSelect` on a pending-question ref — the headline is only the FIRST question's header, so a 3-question capture rendered exactly like a 1-question one, and a multi-select item has its own byte contract that single-select affordances would offer and the bridge would then refuse. The two filters have OPPOSITE failure directions from the guards they sit beside and that is deliberate: an unfilled mirror, an unmirrored workspace, an unreachable daemon or a stale snapshot all resolve to SHOWING the row, because hiding a real blocked agent is the one failure the feature cannot absorb — while the answer path consults neither liveness nor curation after resolving the captured terminal target, so a question captured before its thread was snoozed stays answerable. `(QUESTION-EXPIRY)` closes the same hole for questions: a pending question on a terminal that no longer exists is settled `stale` and its push retracted through the existing settled-ids wiring, instead of buzzing, counting toward `oldestUnansweredMs` and holding a slot forever. It is held to a HIGHER bar than the tree filter beside it, because `settle(stale)` is terminal and the retraction pulls a notification off the phone: it reads a strict `isProvablyGone` (never `!isLive`) that refuses to read anything into an empty daemon listing at any age — the reaper's rule, not the tree's — passes the row's own `last_attached_at ?? created_at` so a terminal born after the snapshot cannot lose that race, and requires the same verdict on two separate reconcile passes five minutes apart. A flap, an unreachable daemon or a stale snapshot resets the clock rather than condemning anything. The same strict predicate gates the push sender's fire-time re-check, whose `forget()` is equally one-shot: an uncertain verdict there keeps the buzz. `(BRIDGE-AGENT-KIND)` keeps read-side classification consistent: the kind falls back from nullable `definition_id` to the hook's exact `agent_id`. It is not an answer preflight — `(ANSWER-GUARDLESS)` deliberately writes to the captured Claude question's terminal without re-reading mutable binding evidence. Two whole-mirror gates sit in front of every per-row rule, both returning the SAME pass-through curation the bootstrap case does, because a mirror that is not evidence about this machine's sidebar right now must not be filtered with. `(MIRROR-AGE-OUT)` refuses a mirror whose last sync is over 20 minutes old — four of the writer's five-minute heartbeats, so only a genuinely absent renderer reaches it — because every hiding field in those tables is then an opinion from a session that has ended, and `snooze_launch_id` in particular keeps hiding threads the very next launch would have released, with nothing left to release them. `(MIRROR-ORG-GATE)` refuses a mirror written for a different organization: `host.db` is per machine and the mirror inside it is per org, the column had been written and read since the mirror shipped without ever being compared, and since ids do not collide across orgs the practical effect was the project gate hiding the ENTIRE tree. `(PUSH-CURATION-GATE)` extends the same curation to the one companion side effect that never passed through the read API: arming hangs off the capture sink, so a binned, archived, completed or snoozed thread still buzzed the WATCH and the notification then opened a tree that did not contain it — snooze worst of all, since "not now" is exactly a statement about being interrupted. It is asked at FIRE time, on every sweep, rather than once before `schedule` — and that is the correctness of the gate, not a detail of where it sits. Curation is REVOCABLE (a snooze expires by itself; an archive or a bin is undone by hand) while `armPush` runs exactly once, at capture, so declining to arm turned a twenty-minute snooze into six hours of silence for a question the sidebar had long since put back, with no fence row left for anything to reconsider and the tree still showing the question the whole time. Every capture is armed now, restart reconstruction covers all of them unchanged, and the sweep decides only whether THIS sweep may fire, so the buzz lands on the first sweep after the curation lapses. The curation hold and the presence hold are independent `continue`s over the same armed entry — whichever holds, holds, and neither can release what the other is still holding — and both sit ABOVE the one-shot `isStillUnanswered` branch, so the one input that is EXPECTED to change its mind is never answered at the point where the only outcomes are fire-now or forget-forever. Answering is still the only permanent disarm. Every uncertain answer BUZZES: curation disabled, no `workspaces` row, a question the memory-only store has never seen (the restart case, which `isStillUnanswered` owns and logs), or anything thrown while asking, and only a positive non-`show` verdict from an enabled curation holds — cached for `CURATION_RECHECK_MS` and logged once per HOLD EPISODE rather than 1,800 times an hour, because a 2 s sweep over a 6 h hold would otherwise mean ~10,800 synchronous reads of the whole mirror per question and as many identical log lines | `(BRIDGE-SIDEBAR-FILTER)`, `(BRIDGE-LIVENESS)`, `(QUESTION-EXPIRY)`, `(BRIDGE-AGENT-KIND)`, `(MIRROR-AGE-OUT)`, `(MIRROR-ORG-GATE)`, `(PUSH-CURATION-GATE)`, `(REAPER-CORRECTION-CAP)`, `(CURATION-PROVENANCE)`, `(EMIT-OPTIONAL-FIELDS)` |
| Tree freshness the phone can trust | the phone stamps its list 'updated just now' when a heartbeat comes back with `treeStale == false` and counts matching the tree it holds — the desktop asserting, live, that a refetch would return what is already on screen. `treeStale` is derived from `gseq`, and `gseq` moved for exactly ONE reason: a question RESOLVING. So a NEW question was invisible to it, and the counts beside it do not always move either, because `deriveSessionStatus` already reports `needs_input` for a terminal whose binding is latched on `PermissionRequest` — the state left behind by `(QUESTION-EXPIRY)` settling a question stale, or by the window after a desk answer before the next hook event lands. A capture on such a terminal changed nothing either signal could see, so the phone confidently asserted freshness over a list with no tappable card for a live blocked agent, indefinitely. Every transition of the pending set now mints the protocol frame that describes it — `question.pending` on capture, `question.resolved` or `question.stale` on a reconcile settle — so `gseq` moves whenever the tree's most important content does. The frames invent nothing: the resolved branch reads back the provenance the store already stamped and reports `outcome: unknown`, which is the honest member (a `tool_result` proves the tool call ended, not that a human chose an option), the stale branch names the one reason `(QUESTION-EXPIRY)` settles on, and a summary whose terminal no longer resolves in host.db is dropped rather than published with a guessed handle. `answerable` on a broadcast frame is evaluated against `BRIDGE_CAPABILITIES`, because a frame has no device — the per-device narrowing is §9.2's snapshot. A capture is published even when `(PUSH-CURATION-GATE)` will hold the push for it: the two gates answer different questions, and both fail toward telling the user more rather than less. Neither publish can throw into its caller: a capture that succeeded must not become a 500, and a retraction must not be lost, over a freshness signal | `(TREE-FRESHNESS-GSEQ)` |
| A retraction that survives the trip | §13's `x` is one field with one meaning and the client applies it BEFORE it reads `k`: `isExpired(now)` discards the frame, so a retraction stamped with `now` was expired on arrival by construction and every notification it was sent to clear survived on the handset. The retract frame now carries its own TTL measured from creation — a day, sized to outlive a phone that was off the network, in Doze or powered down when the answer landed, and safe to over-size because the client independently drops a retraction naming a notification it no longer shows | `(RETRACT-TTL)` |
| One choke point for a settled question | a settled question is exactly the moment any notification about it must be pulled off the phone (§13.3), and that wiring hung off individual call sites: the desk-answer sink retracted and the reconcile path retracted, while the two remaining routes out of `pending` did not. A REMOTE answer — the whole point of the feature — resolved the record and returned, so the watch kept buzzing about the question the user had just answered ON it; and a SUPERSEDE marked the prior record stale by writing the field directly, leaving a notification pointing at a question the tree had already dropped. `retract()` had zero production callers. Every ending now passes through `settle()`, the only writer of a terminal state, which calls one sink the composition root wires to `push.cancelPending` — so a settle route added later cannot forget, because there is nowhere else to write `resolved`/`stale`. The sink is required, not optional, so a composition root that omits it fails to compile rather than running silent; and a sink that throws is caught and logged rather than propagated, because settling has already happened by then and on the answer path the caller has already typed into a terminal | `(SETTLE-CHOKE-POINT)` |
| A backwards clock cannot latch a hold | two caches in the push path bounded their freshness from ABOVE only, so a wall-clock step backwards (NTP correction, resume) made a stamp the clock has not reached yet read as maximally fresh — and both caches only ever hold things that SUPPRESS. The curation probe's per-question row latched a HOLD, silencing a question whose snooze had already lapsed for as long as the step lasted; and `(MIRROR-AGE-OUT)`'s window — the only thing standing between the phone and a mirror left behind by a renderer that has since quit — passed a future stamp forever, so a quit desktop went on hiding threads from the phone. Negative age is now a cache MISS and an AGE-OUT respectively: each fails in the direction its own contract already names, which is toward buzzing and toward showing | `(CLOCK-STEP-FAILS-OPEN)` |
| The hook does not choose a question's workspace | capture stored `input.workspaceId` — a field of an unauthenticated localhost POST — even though `resolveActiveTerminal` had just returned that terminal's `host_workspace_id` from host.db two statements earlier. That id decides which thread the phone opens and is the one `(PUSH-CURATION-GATE)` asks curation about, so a wrong claim buzzes about, and opens, another thread. The derived value is stored and a mismatch is logged with the claim beside it — the same rule `(TRANSCRIPT-PATH-DERIVED)` already applies to the other field the hook also claims | `(HOOK-CLAIM-NOT-TRUSTED)` |
| A gone terminal must be seen twice | the push sender's fire-time re-check answered one boolean for two different facts, and acted on both the same way: `forget()` dropped the fence row, so a question dropped on ONE daemon observation could never buzz again, at any later moment, for any reason — and it happened silently. Everything else in this feature holds an irreversible verdict to two observations (`reconcile` before `settle(stale)`, the reaper before correcting a row); this path did not. The check now answers a VERDICT: `settled` is a fact about the record and is acted on at once, while `gone` is one fallible listing and becomes a HOLD — like presence and curation, and asked while the entry is still armed — until the same verdict comes back `PUSH_GONE_CORROBORATION_MS` later, at which point the drop is LOGGED. A terminal that reads live again resets the clock to zero, so a flapping or mid-restart daemon can never accumulate its way to a drop | `(PUSH-GONE-CORROBORATION)` |

Failure: User works at the desk all day; every completed turn while present mints a held alert (agent finishes → user reviews → prompts again → next cycle mints another). PROTOCOL §13.4 documents late delivery but not this accumulation.
Fix: On a "progress" (or any new-cycle) event for a terminal, delete that terminal's held (unsent) alerts — store hostTerminalId on HeldAlert; a new turn on the terminal is the desk-handled signal, same as an answered question.

Defect: Held lifecycle alerts are never superseded or cancelled by later activity on the same terminal — `record()` returns early for outcome "progress", `HeldAlert` does not even store hostTerminalId, and the only exits from "held" are expiry (6h) or send-on-absence.
Failure: User works at the desk all day; every completed turn while present mints a held alert (agent finishes → user reviews → prompts again → next cycle mints another). Stepping away triggers the 2s sweep to fire EVERY accumulated alert — dozens of distinct alertIds → distinct FCM pushes → distinct notification rows on phone AND watch, all describing work already reviewed and superseded. The question path explicitly disarms on "answered at the desk" (push.ts:32 `cancelPending`); lifecycle has no analog, so FEATURES.md's "presence… match blocked-agent push behavior" claim does not hold. PROTOCOL §13.4 documents late delivery but not this accumulation.
Fix: On a "progress" (or any new-cycle) event for a terminal, delete that terminal's held (unsent) alerts — store hostTerminalId on HeldAlert; a new turn on the terminal is the desk-handled signal, same as an answered question.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:

   Previously completed request:

   - Extend project-less Sessions with existing Archive and Snooze behavior.
   - Keep Sessions off the Kanban board.
   - Make Sessions accessible on the custom phone and watch like Projects.
   - Commit and push that work to `main`.
   - Build and download the Windows ARM64 installer.

   Current feature request:

   - Add distinct mobile alerts for:
     - Green-dot state: an agent appears finished and ready for review.
     - Terminal-agent failures/errors.
   - Keep these separate from the existing blocked/red notification.
   - Send them to both:
     - Custom Android phone app.
     - Custom Wear OS watch app.
   - Ready behavior:
     - Alert once for every genuine working → finished transition.
     - A later work cycle re-arms the alert.
   - Error behavior:
     - Only terminal-agent failures.
     - Exclude tool failures, subagent failures, and administrative failures.
     - Alert once per error event.
   - Preserve existing presence and sidebar-curation behavior so alerts are held while the user is at the computer or the workspace is curated off the sidebar.
   - Add a left-sidebar worktree context-menu action:
     - Label: `Mark completed`.
     - Only visible for active, non-main, Kanban-eligible project worktrees.
     - Must behave like dragging the card into Completed.
     - Completed card must appear at the top.
     - The currently open workspace content must stay visible.
   - Keep Sessions off Kanban.
   - Use Opus subagents for implementation and parallelize work.
   - Have Fable, Sol, and Opus review plans and production code.
   - Remove finished agents to keep the status bar clean.
   - Final delivery authorization:
     - Commit and push both repositories to `main`.
     - Build a Windows ARM64 installer.
     - Build a phone APK.
     - Build a watch APK.

   Decisions collected earlier through AskUser:

   - Alert surfaces: phone and custom watch.
   - Ready trigger: once on every genuine transition from working to finished; another work cycle re-arms it.
   - Error scope: terminal-agent failures only.
   - Error repeat policy: once per error event.
   - Mark completed eligibility: active, non-main project worktrees.
   - Current workspace behavior: keep content open.
   - Sidebar/Kanban behavior: exactly match drag-to-Completed.
   - Delivery: commit and push both repositories.
   - Builds: Windows ARM64 installer, phone APK, and watch APK.

2. Key Technical Concepts:

   - Bun/Turbo TypeScript monorepo.
   - Electron desktop main and renderer processes.
   - Bun test runner and Biome.
   - Host-service tRPC notification ingress.
   - SQLite-backed `terminal_agent_bindings` as lifecycle transition source of truth.
   - DB source of truth; no lifecycle JSON sidecar and no schema change.
   - Claude-generated Python hook embedded in a TypeScript template literal.
   - Agent lifecycle events:
     - `Start`
     - `Stop`
     - `Failed`
     - `PermissionRequest`
     - `BackgroundRunning`
     - `SubagentActive`
   - Status-dot priority:
     - red: needs input
     - yellow: working
     - blue: shell/background activity
     - green: ready for review
   - Main-loop `StopFailure` versus subagent/tool failure semantics.
   - Held Codex-companion work after Claude failure.
   - Existing presence and sidebar-curation push gates.
   - Strict, content-free FCM boundary.
   - Versioned push protocols:
     - v1: blocked question/retraction
     - v2: ready/error lifecycle alerts
   - Closed per-version push key sets.
   - Opaque 22-character base64url identifiers.
   - Canonical lifecycle alert identity:
     - First 16 bytes of a SHA-256 digest.
     - Base64url encoded to 22 characters.
   - Android Firebase Messaging Service.
   - Local Android notification channels and fixed local wording.
   - Wear OS `MessageClient` phone-to-watch relay.
   - Best-effort watch delivery while connected; no offline queue.
   - SharedPreferences-backed persistent event-ID dedupe.
   - Android runtime `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` permission checks.
   - TanStack/local collections for sidebar and Kanban persistence.
   - Shared Kanban completion operation used by both drag and context menu.
   - Completed-card snapshot/freeze behavior.
   - Existing Completed sort:
     - newest `completedAt` first
     - `tabOrder` as secondary order
   - Feature marker gate via the fenced `markers` block in `FEATURES.md`.
   - `(REFERR-GATE)` cannot-find-name diagnostics.
   - Entire repository session tracking.
   - GitHub Actions self-repairing Windows ARM64 release workflow.
   - Signed phone/watch release APKs using the same external keystore.

3. Files and Code Sections:

   A. Superset fork repository

   Root:

   `C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\fork-superset-windows-arm64`

   Documentation and feature protection:

   - `C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\fork-superset-windows-arm64\AGENTS.md`

     ```ts
         .update("sc/v2 lifecycle alert\0", "utf8")
         .update(input.kind, "utf8")
     ```

     Why this matters:

     ```ts
       input,
     ```

     ```ts
     export function buildLifecyclePushData(input: {
       alertId: string;
       workspaceId: WorkspaceId;
       kind: "g" | "e";
       expiresAtMs: number;
     }): PushData {
       if (input.kind !== "g" && input.kind !== "e") {
         throw new PushConfigError(
           `lifecycle alert kind must be "g" or "e", got ${String(input.kind)}`,
         );
       }
       if (
         typeof input.alertId !== "string" ||
         !LIFECYCLE_ID_PATTERN.test(input.alertId)
       ) {
         throw new PushConfigError(
           "lifecycle alertId must be 22 base64url characters — refusing to build (possible text leak)",
         );
       }
       if (
         typeof input.workspaceId !== "string" ||
         !LIFECYCLE_ID_PATTERN.test(input.workspaceId)
       ) {
         throw new PushConfigError(
           "lifecycle workspaceId must be 22 base64url characters — refusing to build (possible text leak)",
         );
       }
       if (!Number.isInteger(input.expiresAtMs) || input.expiresAtMs <= 0) {
         throw new PushConfigError("expiresAtMs must be a positive integer");
       }
       return {
         v: "2",
         k: input.kind,
         i: input.alertId,
         w: input.workspaceId,
         x: String(input.expiresAtMs),
       };
     }
     ```

     ```kotlin
     fun parse(data: Map<String, String>): LifecyclePushData? {
         if (PushEnvelope.version(data) != VERSION) return null
         PushEnvelope.requireClosedAndOpaque(data, KEYS, LABEL, "§13.4")

         val kind =
             LifecycleKind.fromWire(required(data, "k"))
                 ?: throw ProtocolException("lifecycle payload 'k' is not a known kind")
         val expiry =
             required(data, "x").toLongOrNull()
                 ?: throw ProtocolException("lifecycle payload 'x' is not a number")

         return LifecyclePushData(
             kind = kind,
             eventId = Ids.requireOpaque16(required(data, "i"), "lifecycle.i"),
             workspaceId = Ids.requireOpaque16(required(data, "w"), "lifecycle.w"),
             expiresAtMs = expiry,
         )
     }
     ```

skills.content:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

BLUEPRINT — ready-for-review + terminal-agent-error alerts (phone + watch). Read-only review of both repos complete. All paths absolute; every claim cited from code I read.

AMBIGUITY FLAGGED UP FRONT
- "Terminal agent failure": only observable server-side signal is hook eventType mapped to "Failed" (StopFailure — Claude API-error hook) at fork-superset-windows-arm64/packages/host-service/src/events/map-event-type.ts:100-106. Assumption made: "Failed" + no "Start" within a 120s grace window = terminal failure. A rate-limited agent alerts after 120s even though auto-resume may revive it hours later — I judge that correct-to-alert, but it is a semantics decision the user may want to override.
- "Once per work cycle": defined as Start-latched — armed on mapped "Start", fired on first "Stop" while armed, re-armed only by next "Start". No timer heuristics.

1. RECOMMENDED APPROACH
Hook-event-driven alert engine inside the companion bridge; two new data-only FCM kinds ("g" ready, "e" error) carrying only opaque handles; presence rule = present→DROP, away→fire immediately (no hold, no fence); phone enriches from tree fetch; watch gets alerts via the existing explicit Data Layer path.

Key design decisions and why:
- Source of truth = notifications.hook router. It already receives every mapped lifecycle event with terminalId + originWorkspaceId resolved from host.db (packages/host-service/src/trpc/router/notifications/notifications.ts:171-296, broadcast at :260, forwardCompanionCapture at :283). Zero renderer involvement — the renderer "review/green" axis is renderer-only localStorage (apps/desktop/src/renderer/stores/v2-notifications/store.ts:89 AGENT_AXIS_PRIORITY) and unreadable from the bridge, so deriving green from hook Start/Stop is the only server-side option.
- Seam = extend the existing fork-only sink file, NOT the EventBus. EventBus.broadcastAgentLifecycle only fans to WS sockets, no in-process listeners (packages/host-service/src/events/event-bus.ts:185-189); adding onAgentLifecycle would grow an upstream-owned file's merge surface. companion-question-sink.ts is the established fork seam (setCompanionQuestionSink throws on double install, companion-question-sink.ts:99; forward called strictly after dot work per (COMPANION-CAPTURE-HOOK) comment notifications.ts:278-288). Add forwardCompanionLifecycle beside forwardCompanionCapture: one import name + one call line added in notifications.ts, everything else fork-only.
- Presence rule differs from red deliberately: PROTOCOL.md 13.2 holds question pushes indefinitely because a blocked agent stays blocked. Ready/error info decays — user at desk sees the dot; a buzz hours later on walking away is noise. present→drop kills the entire fence/orphan/restart-reconstruction machinery (push-fence.ts, push.ts fence reconstruction ~1737) for alerts. PresenceStore.present(nowMs) verdict is a one-call check (packages/host-service/src/companion/presence.ts:114-141); "resume-settling" verdict counts as present (machine just woke = user there) — acceptable drop.
- Transport reuse, not scheduler reuse: createPushSender's deliver/broadcast already does OAuth mint, 4-attempt backoff, dead-token pruning, auth-fault raising (push.ts:1314-1421). - Add distinct mobile lifecycle alerts for:

Current semantics:
- `HeldAlert` stores `hostTerminalId`.
- New `progress` for a terminal cancels earlier held alerts for that terminal.
- `session-end` also cancels held alerts for that terminal.
- This prevents an all-day desk session from releasing many stale alerts later.
- Ready requires previous:
  - `Start`
  - `SubagentActive`
  - `BackgroundRunning`
- Error additionally allows previous `PermissionRequest`.
- Repeated `Stop`/`Failed` is silent because the previous persisted event is no longer active.
- `producerEventId` is now used for bounded duplicate POST protection.
- Malformed producer dedupe ID logs and processes rather than dropping a real alert.
- Send claims the canonical held entry atomically before awaiting.
- Overlapping sweeps re-read canonical map state and cannot send one alert twice.
- Failed delivery returns the alert to held state.
- Retry backoff:
  - starts at 30 seconds
  - doubles
  - caps at 15 minutes
- `no-devices` is retryable during the alert TTL.
- Only at least one accepted device marks the alert delivered.
- Bounded pruning logs loudly when it evicts an unsent held alert.

skills.name: simplify
skills.content:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).
